questions.text: A company wants to migrate an on-premises SFTP server storing data on NFS to AWS. The target is an EC2 instance using an EFS file system with 200 GB of data. Which combination of steps automates this task?

options.A: Launch the EC2 instance into the same Availability Zone as the EFS file system.
options.B: Install an AWS DataSync agent in the on-premises data center.
options.C: Create a secondary Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume on the EC2 instance for the data.
options.D: Manually use an operating system copy command to push the data to the EC2 instance.
options.E: Use AWS DataSync to create a suitable location configuration for the on-premises SFTP server.

explanations.A: EFS is a regional service and can be mounted from any AZ in the same region, so launching the EC2 instance in the same AZ is optional, not required.
explanations.B: Installing an AWS DataSync agent in the on-premises environment enables automated, secure, and efficient data transfer to AWS.
explanations.C: A secondary EBS volume is unnecessary since the target is EFS, which can scale storage automatically.
explanations.D: Manual OS copy commands do not automate the migration and are error-prone for repeated or large-scale transfers.
explanations.E: DataSync location configuration defines the source (on-premises SFTP) and destination (EFS) endpoints, enabling automated and efficient migration.

questions.text: A company has an AWS Glue ETL job that processes XML data in an S3 bucket daily. Each run, Glue processes all data, including old data. How can the job be modified to prevent reprocessing old data?

options.A: Edit the job to use job bookmarks.
options.B: Edit the job to delete data after the data is processed.
options.C: Edit the job by setting the NumberOfWorkers field to 1.
options.D: Use a FindMatches machine learning (ML) transform.

explanations.A: AWS Glue job bookmarks track previously processed data and process only new or changed data in subsequent runs, preventing reprocessing of old data.
explanations.B: Deleting data after processing is not ideal as it risks losing historical data and may violate retention requirements.
explanations.C: Changing the number of workers affects performance but does not prevent reprocessing of old data.
explanations.D: FindMatches is a machine learning transform for deduplication and does not prevent reprocessing of old data.

questions.text:
A company uses a popular content management system (CMS) for its corporate website. However, the required patching and maintenance are burdensome. The company is redesigning its website and wants a new solution. The website will be updated four times a year and does not need to have any dynamic content available. The solution must provide high scalability and enhanced security.
Which combination of changes will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose two.)

options.A: Configure Amazon CloudFront in front of the website to use HTTPS functionality.
options.B: Deploy an AWS WAF web ACL in front of the website to provide HTTPS functionality.
options.C: Create and deploy an AWS Lambda function to manage and serve the website content.
options.D: Create the new website and an Amazon S3 bucket. Deploy the website on the S3 bucket with static website hosting enabled.
options.E: Create the new website. Deploy the website by using an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer

explanations.A: **Amazon CloudFront is essential for several reasons:** 1) It serves as a global Content Delivery Network (CDN), providing **high scalability** and **high performance** by caching content at edge locations worldwide. 2) It is the standard way to provide **enhanced security** (DDoS protection, encryption) and **HTTPS functionality** for an S3 static website, as S3 static website endpoints do not natively support HTTPS with a custom domain name. 3) It further reduces operational overhead by taking the load off the origin.
explanations.B: AWS WAF provides security, but it does **not** provide HTTPS/SSL termination in the way that CloudFront does, nor does it provide CDN acceleration and global scalability. While WAF can be *used* with CloudFront to enhance security, it's not the primary component for enabling HTTPS and scalability for a static site.
explanations.C: AWS Lambda is designed for running dynamic, serverless code. Since the website contains **no dynamic content**, using Lambda to serve content would introduce unnecessary operational complexity and cost compared to the simple S3 static hosting feature.
explanations.D: **Amazon S3 static website hosting** is the solution that meets the core requirements of high scalability, no maintenance/patching, and **least operational overhead** for a website with only static content. Since the old system's patching/maintenance was burdensome, moving to a fully managed, serverless storage solution like S3 eliminates all OS-level maintenance.
explanations.E: Using an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances, even behind an ALB, is the traditional **heavy-lift** approach. It requires managing AMIs, patches, scaling configurations, and load balancers. This is the opposite of the requirement for the **LEAST operational overhead**, especially since the content is static.

questions.text:
A company hosts an online shopping application that stores all orders in an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Single-AZ DB instance. Management wants to eliminate single points of failure and has asked a solutions architect to recommend an approach to minimize database downtime without requiring any changes to the application code.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Convert the existing database instance to a Multi-AZ deployment by modifying the database instance and specifying the Multi-AZ option.
options.B: Create a new RDS Multi-AZ deployment. Take a snapshot of the current RDS instance and restore the new Multi-AZ deployment with the snapshot.
options.C: Create a read-only replica of the PostgreSQL database in another Availability Zone. Use Amazon Route 53 weighted record sets to distribute requests across the databases.
options.D: Place the RDS for PostgreSQL database in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group with a minimum group size of two. Use Amazon Route 53 weighted record sets to distribute requests across instances.

explanations.A: Correct. Converting an existing RDS instance to Multi-AZ provides synchronous standby replication and automatic failover with minimal downtime and no application changes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Restoring from a snapshot introduces additional downtime and operational overhead compared to in-place conversion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Read replicas are not designed for write failover and Route 53 weighted routing does not handle database write consistency.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Amazon RDS cannot be placed in an EC2 Auto Scaling group, and this approach is not supported.
explanations.correct: Multi-AZ deployment is the AWS-recommended approach for eliminating single points of failure in RDS with minimal downtime.

questions.text: A solutions architect needs to implement a solution to reduce a company's storage costs. All the company's data is in the Amazon S3 Standard storage class. The company must keep all data for at least 25 years. Data from the most recent 2 years must be highly available and immediately retrievable. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Set up an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive immediately.
options.B: Set up an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 2 years.
options.C: Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering. Activate the archiving option to ensure that data is archived in S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
options.D: Set up an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) immediately and to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 2 years.

explanations.A: Transitioning objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive immediately does not meet the requirement that data from the most recent 2 years must be **highly available and immediately retrievable** (in milliseconds). Data in Deep Archive has retrieval times measured in hours.
explanations.B: This solution transitions data to the low-cost archive tier after 2 years, meeting the long-term retention requirement. However, it keeps the data in S3 Standard for the first 2 years, which is more expensive than necessary for data that becomes infrequently accessed after 2 years but doesn't transition to the lowest possible cost tier automatically.
explanations.C: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between S3 Standard (for frequent access) and S3 Standard-IA (for infrequent access) tiers based on access patterns, ensuring high availability and immediate retrieval for the active data. Activating the optional Archive Access Tier (using Glacier or Deep Archive) ensures that data that has not been accessed for 90 days is automatically moved to S3 Glacier Deep Archive, providing the lowest storage cost while still meeting the 25-year retention and immediate retrieval requirement for the most recent 2 years.
explanations.D: S3 One Zone-IA is not highly available (it can lose data in the event of an Availability Zone destruction) and is typically not recommended unless cost savings must be maximized over durability. The requirement for the most recent 2 years is **highly available and immediately retrievable**, which S3 Standard or S3 Intelligent-Tiering provides better than S3 One Zone-IA.
explanations.correct: S3 Intelligent-Tiering is the most cost-effective and operationally simple solution because it automatically optimizes storage costs while meeting the high availability and immediate retrieval requirements for the most recent data, and the Deep Archive setting meets the long-term, low-cost retention requirement.

questions.text: A company has 700 TB of backup data stored in network attached storage (NAS) in its data center. This backup data need to be accessible for infrequent regulatory requests and must be retained 7 years. The company has decided to migrate this backup data from its data center to AWS. The migration must be complete within 1 month. The company has 500 Mbps of dedicated bandwidth on its public internet connection available for data transfer. What should a solutions architect do to migrate and store the data at the LOWEST cost?

options.A: Order AWS Snowball devices to transfer the data. Use a lifecycle policy to transition the files to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
options.B: Deploy a VPN connection between the data center and Amazon VPC. Use the AWS CLI to copy the data from on premises to Amazon S3 Glacier.
options.C: Provision a 500 Mbps AWS Direct Connect connection and transfer the data to Amazon S3. Use a lifecycle policy to transition the files to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
options.D: Use AWS DataSync to transfer the data and deploy a DataSync agent on premises. Use the DataSync task to copy files from the on-premises NAS storage to Amazon S3 Glacier.

explanations.A: The $700 	ext{ TB}$ of data cannot be transferred over a $500 	ext{ Mbps}$ connection within the required 1 month (it would take approx. 130 days). **AWS Snowball** is the appropriate service for transferring hundreds of terabytes within a strict time limit (physical transfer). **S3 Glacier Deep Archive** is the most cost-effective storage class for data that is rarely accessed (infrequent regulatory requests) and retained for long periods (7 years). This combination meets all requirements at the lowest cost.
explanations.B: Transferring 700 TB over any 500 Mbps connection (public internet or VPN) will take too long (approx. 130 days), violating the 1-month deadline. AWS CLI is generally not optimized for large-scale migrations like DataSync or Snowball.
explanations.C: A 500 Mbps AWS Direct Connect connection still has the same bandwidth limitation (approx. 130 days for 700 TB), violating the 1-month deadline. Additionally, Direct Connect has recurring monthly costs that would likely make the solution more expensive than using Snowball for a one-time migration.
explanations.D: AWS DataSync is excellent for online transfers but is bottlenecked by the 500 Mbps connection, violating the 1-month deadline. S3 Glacier, while cost-effective, cannot be directly set as the target for DataSync; the target must be S3 Standard/IA/Intelligent-Tiering, requiring a lifecycle policy afterward (similar to option A), but the transfer method is too slow.
explanations.correct: For massive data migrations (over 100 TB) with strict time constraints, the AWS Snow Family (Snowball) is required to meet the deadline. S3 Glacier Deep Archive offers the lowest storage cost for data that is infrequently accessed and needs long-term retention.

questions.text:
A solutions architect is using Amazon S3 to design the storage architecture of a new digital media application. The media files must be resilient to the loss of an Availability Zone. Some files are accessed frequently while other files are rarely accessed in an unpredictable pattern. The solutions architect must minimize the costs of storing and retrieving the media files.
Which storage option meets these requirements?

options.A: S3 Standard
options.B: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
options.C: S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA)
options.D: S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA)

explanations.A: Incorrect. S3 Standard is suitable for frequently accessed data and is resilient across multiple AZs. However, it is the most expensive of the general-purpose classes and does not meet the requirement to minimize costs for data that is rarely accessed.
explanations.B: Correct. S3 Intelligent-Tiering is designed for data with changing or unpredictable access patterns. It automatically moves objects between two access tiers (Frequent and Infrequent Access) based on access patterns, which helps minimize storage costs while retaining multi-AZ resilience, satisfying the requirement to be resilient to the loss of an Availability Zone.
explanations.C: Incorrect. S3 Standard-IA is designed for data that is *infrequently* accessed, but it has a retrieval charge, and moving data to it requires a lifecycle policy or manual action. Since the access pattern is described as 'unpredictable' with 'some files accessed frequently,' using S3 Standard-IA for all data could result in high retrieval costs for the frequently accessed files.
explanations.D: Incorrect. S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) is designed for data that is rarely accessed and is stored in a single Availability Zone (AZ). This violates the core requirement that the media files must be **resilient to the loss of an Availability Zone**.
explanations.correct: S3 Intelligent-Tiering provides the best balance of cost minimization for unpredictable access patterns and resilience. It automatically moves data to a lower-cost tier when it's not accessed for 30 consecutive days, but it maintains the high durability and availability of storing data across multiple Availability Zones, ensuring resilience against the loss of an AZ.

questions.text:
A solutions architect is designing a new API using Amazon API Gateway that will receive requests from users. The volume of requests is highly variable; several hours can pass without receiving a single request. The data processing will take place asynchronously, but should be completed within a few seconds after a request is made.
Which compute service should the solutions architect have the API invoke to deliver the requirements at the lowest cost?

options.A: An AWS Glue job
options.B: An AWS Lambda function
options.C: A containerized service hosted in Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS)
options.D: A containerized service hosted in Amazon ECS with Amazon EC2

explanations.A: Incorrect. AWS Glue is a fully managed extract, transform, and load (ETL) service designed for large-scale data processing jobs. It is optimized for batch-style processing that takes minutes to hours, not near-real-time responses within a few seconds. The associated startup time and cost structure are not suitable for a low-volume, low-latency API backend.
explanations.B: Correct. **AWS Lambda** is the most cost-efficient choice for highly variable, intermittent workloads. Its pricing model is based purely on the number of requests and the execution duration, billed per millisecond. Since the API will often go hours without a request, Lambda incurs **zero cost** during idle time. For the brief, fast (few seconds) processing time, its usage-based pricing minimizes cost compared to services that require continuous uptime.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Amazon EKS requires paying a fixed, continuous hourly charge for the control plane (approximately $0.10/hour per cluster), regardless of whether the cluster is processing requests or not. This fixed cost, combined with the cost of the underlying compute (even Fargate), makes it significantly more expensive than Lambda for low-volume, intermittent traffic.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hosting a service on Amazon ECS with **Amazon EC2** requires provisioning and running EC2 instances continuously to handle potential requests. Even during the 'several hours' of zero activity, the company would pay for the idle EC2 instance time, making it significantly more expensive than a serverless, pay-per-use model for this specific traffic pattern.
explanations.correct: AWS Lambda is the ideal compute choice for highly variable, intermittent workloads due to its 'pay-for-use' billing model (per request and per millisecond of compute time). Because the volume is highly variable and low, and processing is fast (a few seconds), Lambda's **zero idle cost** model offers the lowest total cost compared to constantly running container platforms (ECS/EKS on EC2/Fargate) or batch processing services (Glue).

questions.text:
A company runs an application on a group of Amazon Linux EC2 instances. For compliance reasons, the company must retain all application log files for 7 years. The log files will be analyzed by a reporting tool that must be able to access all the files concurrently.
Which storage solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)
options.B: Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS)
options.C: Amazon EC2 instance store
options.D: Amazon S3

explanations.A: Incorrect. Amazon EBS provides block storage, which is suitable for a single EC2 instance's primary volume. EBS volumes are expensive for long-term archival compared to object storage, and they cannot be easily shared or accessed concurrently by many EC2 instances or a centralized reporting tool.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Amazon EFS provides a scalable, shared file system that allows concurrent access from multiple EC2 instances. While it meets the concurrent access requirement, EFS is significantly more expensive than Amazon S3 for petabyte-scale, long-term retention/archival of data like log files. EFS is primarily optimized for low-latency, shared file storage for active workloads.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Amazon EC2 Instance Store provides temporary, block-level storage physically attached to the host computer. Data on the instance store is lost when the instance is stopped or terminated, making it unsuitable for the 7-year retention compliance requirement.
explanations.D: Correct. **Amazon S3** (Object Storage) is the standard, most cost-effective service for storing massive amounts of unstructured data, including application logs, over long periods (7 years). S3 offers superior durability, scalability, and is easily accessible by various reporting and analytics tools (concurrent access via API). Furthermore, S3 Lifecycle policies can be used to automatically transition the logs to even lower-cost tiers like S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive after a few months, further minimizing storage costs while meeting the retention requirement.
explanations.correct: Amazon S3 is the most cost-effective, durable, and scalable solution for long-term retention of massive log files. It meets the concurrent access requirement because objects can be accessed simultaneously via API by multiple users/tools. Lifecycle policies can be leveraged to move data to the S3 Glacier storage classes (like Deep Archive) for extreme cost savings for the majority of the 7-year period.

questions.text: A company needs to retain its AWS CloudTrail logs for 3 years. The company is enforcing CloudTrail across a set of AWS accounts by using AWS Organizations from the parent account. The CloudTrail target S3 bucket is configured with S3 Versioning enabled. An S3 Lifecycle policy is in place to delete current objects after 3 years. After the fourth year of use of the S3 bucket, the S3 bucket metrics show that the number of objects has continued to rise. However, the number of new CloudTrail logs that are delivered to the S3 bucket has remained consistent. Which solution will delete objects that are older than 3 years in the MOST cost-effective manner?

options.A: Configure the organization’s centralized CloudTrail trail to expire objects after 3 years.
options.B: Configure the S3 Lifecycle policy to delete previous versions as well as current versions.
options.C: Create an AWS Lambda function to enumerate and delete objects from Amazon S3 that are older than 3 years.
options.D: Configure the parent account as the owner of all objects that are delivered to the S3 bucket.

explanations.A: CloudTrail itself does not have a configuration to expire or delete the S3 objects it delivers. It is a delivery mechanism. Object retention is managed by the S3 Bucket Lifecycle Policy.
explanations.B: This is the most cost-effective and appropriate solution. Since S3 Versioning is enabled, and the object count is rising, it implies that the non-current (previous) versions are accumulating. S3 Lifecycle policies must be configured with a separate rule to expire/delete non-current object versions after a specified number of days (e.g., 3 years + 1 day). This utilizes a native, serverless S3 feature.
explanations.C: Creating an AWS Lambda function to enumerate and delete objects is a costly, complex, and high-overhead solution compared to the native S3 Lifecycle policy. It would require managing code, execution time costs, and API calls (DELETE, LIST), which is significantly less cost-effective.
explanations.D: Object ownership is related to access control (ACLs) and cross-account bucket policies, which is a consideration for centralized logging but has no direct effect on automatically deleting objects after a certain retention period. The S3 Lifecycle policy manages retention regardless of the object owner.
explanations.correct: The symptom (rising object count with consistent delivery rate) combined with the configuration (Versioning enabled, Lifecycle policy only for current objects) points directly to the retention of non-current object versions. The simplest and MOST cost-effective way to manage object retention at scale in S3 is by using the native S3 Lifecycle policy for both current and non-current versions.

questions.text:
A company is developing a marketing communications service that targets mobile app users. The company needs to send confirmation messages with Short Message Service (SMS) to its users. The users must be able to reply to the SMS messages. The company must store the responses for a year for analysis.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.A: Create an Amazon Connect contact flow to send the SMS messages. Use AWS Lambda to process the responses.
options.B: Build an Amazon Pinpoint journey. Configure Amazon Pinpoint to send events to an Amazon Kinesis data stream for analysis and archiving.
options.C: Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) to distribute the SMS messages. Use AWS Lambda to process the responses.
options.D: Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) FIFO topic. Subscribe an Amazon Kinesis data stream to the SNS topic for analysis and archiving.

explanations.A: Amazon Connect is primarily for call centers (voice and chat) and while it has SMS features, it is an overly complex and costly solution for simple application-to-person (A2P) marketing communications and two-way SMS. Amazon Pinpoint is the dedicated service for this use case.
explanations.B: Amazon Pinpoint is the AWS service specifically designed for marketing communications, including sending bulk SMS and managing **two-way SMS** (allowing user replies). Pinpoint is configured to stream all engagement events (including message deliveries and user responses/replies) to an integrated streaming service like Amazon Kinesis Data Streams (or Amazon S3 via Kinesis Firehose). Kinesis can then pipe the responses to S3 for cost-effective 1-year archival and to an analytics service (like Amazon Athena or OpenSearch) for analysis, meeting all requirements.
explanations.C: Amazon SQS is a queueing service for decoupling components; it does not have native functionality for sending or receiving external SMS messages. This option is fundamentally incorrect for the SMS use case.
explanations.D: Amazon SNS is a Pub/Sub service that can send one-way SMS messages, but it is not the primary service for marketing communications or for easily configuring **two-way SMS**. While Pinpoint can use SNS internally to handle inbound messages, Amazon Pinpoint is the higher-level service that provides the integrated platform for managing the entire campaign, user responses, and analytics streams.
explanations.correct: Amazon Pinpoint is the correct customer engagement and communications service for sending confirmation SMS messages and enabling two-way communication. Pinpoint's ability to stream all message events (including replies) to Amazon Kinesis provides the necessary mechanism for near real-time analysis and long-term storage in Amazon S3 for archival.
explanations.diagram_query: Amazon Pinpoint two-way SMS architecture with Kinesis

questions.text: A company is storing backup files by using Amazon S3 Standard storage. The files are accessed frequently for 1 month. However, the files are not accessed after 1 month. The company must keep the files indefinitely. Which storage solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Configure S3 Intelligent-Tiering to automatically migrate objects.
options.B: Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration to transition objects from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 month.
options.C: Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration to transition objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 1 month.
options.D: Create an S3 Lifecycle configuration to transition objects from S3 Standard to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) after 1 month.

explanations.A: S3 Intelligent-Tiering is best for **unknown, changing, or unpredictable** access patterns. Since the access pattern here is **well-defined** (frequent for 1 month, then not accessed), and S3 Intelligent-Tiering incurs a small per-object monitoring fee, it is not the *most* cost-effective solution compared to a targeted Lifecycle policy that moves data directly to the cheapest archive class.
explanations.B: This is the **MOST cost-effective** solution. **S3 Glacier Deep Archive** is the lowest-cost storage class offered by AWS, designed specifically for long-term retention (indefinitely) of data that is rarely or never accessed (matching the 'not accessed after 1 month' requirement). Using an S3 Lifecycle policy automates the movement to this lower-cost class after the initial 30 days of frequent access.
explanations.C: S3 Standard-IA is designed for data accessed **infrequently but still requiring millisecond access** when needed. Since the requirement is that the files are **not accessed** after 1 month, S3 Standard-IA is significantly more expensive than S3 Glacier Deep Archive for long-term storage.
explanations.D: S3 One Zone-IA is similar to S3 Standard-IA but is stored in a single Availability Zone, making it cheaper than S3 Standard-IA but less durable. Critically, it is still much more expensive than S3 Glacier Deep Archive and does not represent the **MOST** cost-effective solution for data that is never expected to be retrieved.
explanations.correct: For data that must be kept **indefinitely** and is **not accessed** after a short initial period, **S3 Glacier Deep Archive** offers the lowest storage cost. An **S3 Lifecycle policy** is the correct mechanism to automatically move the objects from the more expensive S3 Standard class after the initial 1-month period.

questions.text: A company wants to experiment with individual AWS accounts for its engineer team. The company wants to be notified as soon as the Amazon EC2 instance usage for a given month exceeds a specific threshold for each account. What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Use Cost Explorer to create a daily report of costs by service. Filter the report by EC2 instances. Configure Cost Explorer to send an Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) notification when a threshold is exceeded.
options.B: Use Cost Explorer to create a monthly report of costs by service. Filter the report by EC2 instances. Configure Cost Explorer to send an Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) notification when a threshold is exceeded.
options.C: Use AWS Budgets to create a cost budget for each account. Set the period to monthly. Set the scope to EC2 instances. Set an alert threshold for the budget. Configure an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to receive a notification when a threshold is exceeded.
options.D: Use AWS Cost and Usage Reports to create a report with hourly granularity. Integrate the report data with Amazon Athena. Use Amazon EventBridge to schedule an Athena query. Configure an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to receive a notification when a threshold is exceeded.

explanations.A: Cost Explorer is for analysis and visualization; while it can create reports, its primary function is not to send real-time, threshold-based alerts. Moreover, sending custom notifications via Amazon SES would require additional setup and cost (if not using the free tier or if exceeding limits), making this less cost-effective than the managed solution.
explanations.B: Similar to option A, Cost Explorer is not the dedicated alerting service. While it can show forecasted or actual spend, it does not offer the simple, integrated, and cost-effective alerting mechanism provided by AWS Budgets. AWS Budgets is the purpose-built, free service for this task.
explanations.C: AWS Budgets is the **most cost-effective** and purpose-built service for this requirement. It allows you to set custom thresholds based on **cost** or **usage** (in this case, EC2 usage) with a monthly period and scope it to a specific service (EC2). Notifications via Amazon SNS are a standard, automated, and free feature of Budgets (for up to 10 alerts per month in the free tier, and SNS is generally very low cost), making this the MOST cost-effective and appropriate solution.
explanations.D: This solution is overly complex and requires multiple paid services (CUR storage in S3, Athena queries, EventBridge scheduling, Lambda if needed for deeper logic). While it provides the highest granularity, it is not the **MOST cost-effective** way to meet the simple requirement of getting a monthly notification when a threshold is exceeded. AWS Budgets is free and much simpler.

questions.text: A company observes an increase in Amazon EC2 costs in its most recent bill. The billing team notices unwanted vertical scaling of instance types for a couple of EC2 instances. A solutions architect needs to create a graph comparing the last 2 months of EC2 costs and perform an in-depth analysis to identify the root cause of the vertical scaling. How should the solutions architect generate the information with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Use AWS Budgets to create a budget report and compare EC2 costs based on instance types.
options.B: Use Cost Explorer's granular filtering feature to perform an in-depth analysis of EC2 costs based on instance types.
options.C: Use graphs from the AWS Billing and Cost Management dashboard to compare EC2 costs based on instance types for the last 2 months.
options.D: Use AWS Cost and Usage Reports to create a report and send it to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon QuickSight with Amazon S3 as a source to generate an interactive graph based on instance types.

explanations.A: AWS Budgets is designed for setting thresholds and receiving alerts, not for granular, retrospective, and in-depth cost analysis and comparison across multiple months based on resource types.
explanations.B: Cost Explorer is the dedicated, built-in AWS tool for visualizing, understanding, and managing AWS costs and usage over time. It offers granular filtering by service (EC2), usage type (instance type), and time frame (last 2 months) to perform the required in-depth analysis and generate comparison graphs **with zero setup or operational overhead**.
explanations.C: The AWS Billing and Cost Management dashboard provides a high-level overview. It lacks the necessary granular filtering and comparison capabilities to drill down specifically into EC2 instance types over the last 2 months to perform an **in-depth analysis** and identify the root cause, which is a key requirement.
explanations.D: AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) combined with Amazon QuickSight is a powerful solution for complex, custom analysis. However, it requires significant setup (enabling CUR, configuring S3 storage, setting up QuickSight dashboards and data sources), which violates the requirement for the **LEAST operational overhead**.
explanations.correct: Cost Explorer is a fully managed, zero-setup service designed specifically for cost analysis, comparison, and granular filtering by instance type and date range, making it the most appropriate and operationally efficient tool for this task.

questions.text: A company previously migrated its data warehouse solution to AWS. The company also has an AWS Direct Connect connection. Corporate office users query the data warehouse using a visualization tool. The average size of a query returned by the data warehouse is 50 MB and each webpage sent by the visualization tool is approximately 500 KB. Result sets returned by the data warehouse are not cached. Which solution provides the LOWEST data transfer egress cost for the company?

options.A: Host the visualization tool on premises and query the data warehouse directly over the internet.
options.B: Host the visualization tool in the same AWS Region as the data warehouse. Access it over the internet.
options.C: Host the visualization tool on premises and query the data warehouse directly over a Direct Connect connection at a location in the same AWS Region.
options.D: Host the visualization tool in the same AWS Region as the data warehouse and access it over a Direct Connect connection at a location in the same Region.

explanations.A: This requires two major types of egress charges: 1) The **large** data warehouse query results (50 MB) must egress from AWS to the internet, which has the **highest per-GB rate** (typically $0.09/GB, after the free tier). 2) The visualization tool's webpage (500 KB) must egress from on-premises to the internet (free inbound to AWS) and then the query results go out via the internet. This is the most expensive egress path for high-volume data egress.
explanations.B: This solution keeps the entire communication within the AWS Region. Data transfer between services within the same AWS Region is generally **free**, as long as they are in the same Availability Zone (AZ) or using private IP addresses. Even if they are in different AZs (cross-AZ traffic), the charge is very low (around $0.01/GB). This completely avoids the high egress charges associated with Direct Connect (DTO) or the public internet, making it the lowest-cost solution. The access over the internet only applies to the user viewing the visualization tool's webpage, which is low volume and uses the free 100GB monthly tier for internet egress. The high-volume query result data (50 MB) stays in AWS.
explanations.C: This uses the Direct Connect (DX) path, which has a **lower per-GB egress rate** than the public internet (typically around $0.02/GB, depending on the region). While it is cheaper than option A, it is still a significant charge for every 50 MB query result that must be transferred out of AWS, and it includes the hourly port fee for the DX connection. This is more expensive than keeping the transfer entirely within the AWS cloud.
explanations.D: This solution makes no sense and introduces unnecessary cost. Hosting the tool in the AWS Region means the tool and the data warehouse can communicate privately within AWS. Routing this private traffic back through a Direct Connect connection (which is designed to connect AWS to **on-premises**) and then back into AWS would be complex, nonsensical, and expensive, incurring Direct Connect egress charges for what should be free internal traffic.
explanations.correct: The LOWEST data transfer egress cost is achieved when the high-volume data (50 MB query results) never leaves the AWS network. By placing the visualization tool in the same AWS Region as the data warehouse, the 50 MB data transfer occurs as intra-region/intra-AZ traffic, which is either free or has the lowest possible charge (cross-AZ, $\sim$ $0.01/GB$), which is significantly cheaper than both Direct Connect egress ($\sim$ $0.02/GB$) and public internet egress ($\sim$ $0.09/GB$).

references: AWS Data Transfer Pricing documentation (Intra-region is lowest cost, followed by Direct Connect, then Internet).

questions.text: A company is launching an application on AWS. The application uses an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to direct traffic to at least two Amazon EC2 instances in a single target group. The instances are in an Auto Scaling group for each environment. The company requires a development environment and a production environment. The production environment will have periods of high traffic. Which solution will configure the development environment MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Reconfigure the target group in the development environment to have only one EC2 instance as a target.
options.B: Change the ALB balancing algorithm to least outstanding requests.
options.C: Reduce the size of the EC2 instances in both environments.
options.D: Reduce the maximum number of EC2 instances in the development environment’s Auto Scaling group.

explanations.A: This only manually changes the target group configuration, but the Auto Scaling group (ASG) would likely still try to maintain a minimum desired capacity of two instances, and it does not limit the maximum instances that can be launched, which is the primary driver of cost for a dev environment.
explanations.B: Changing the load balancing algorithm addresses how traffic is distributed, which is related to performance, not cost-effectiveness. The default is round-robin, and changing it will not reduce the number of EC2 instances or the cost of the environment.
explanations.C: Reducing the size of EC2 instances in **both** environments is risky. The production environment has periods of high traffic and needs appropriately sized instances for performance. Reducing the size globally could impact production performance and availability, which is not acceptable.
explanations.D: The cost of an Auto Scaling group is primarily driven by the number of EC2 instances running. By reducing the **maximum number of EC2 instances** allowed in the development environment's Auto Scaling group, the system is prevented from scaling up unnecessarily during testing or unexpected demand. This directly controls and limits the maximum monthly EC2 usage and cost for the non-production environment, making it the **MOST cost-effective** configuration change that also aligns with the typical low-traffic nature of a development environment.
explanations.correct: Cost-effectiveness is achieved by limiting resource consumption. Setting a lower maximum capacity in the ASG for the development environment directly caps the maximum number of expensive EC2 instances that can be launched, thereby controlling the overall operational cost.

references: AWS Well-Architected Framework: Cost Optimization Pillar, Principle 1: Adopt a Consumption Model.

questions.text: A company hosts multiple production applications. One of the applications consists of resources from Amazon EC2, AWS Lambda, Amazon RDS, Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), and Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) across multiple AWS Regions. All company resources are tagged with a tag name of “application” and a value that corresponds to each application. A solutions architect must provide the quickest solution for identifying all of the tagged components. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.A: Use AWS CloudTrail to generate a list of resources with the application tag.
options.B: Use the AWS CLI to query each service across all Regions to report the tagged components.
options.C: Run a query in Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to report on the components with the application tag.
options.D: Run a query with the AWS Resource Groups Tag Editor to report on the resources globally with the application tag.

explanations.A: AWS CloudTrail records API activity (who did what, when). It is not designed to provide a real-time inventory of currently existing resources or to quickly query resources based on their tags. This would require complex and slow log processing.
explanations.B: Using the AWS CLI to query *each service* and manually iterate through *all Regions* is labor-intensive, slow, error-prone, and requires custom scripting. This approach maximizes operational overhead and is not the *quickest* solution.
explanations.C: CloudWatch Logs Insights is for analyzing log data, such as VCP Flow Logs or Lambda logs. It does not provide a centralized inventory of all deployed AWS resources and their current tags. This solution is incorrect for inventory management.
explanations.D: The **AWS Resource Groups Tag Editor** (which uses the Resource Groups Tagging API) is the dedicated, centralized service designed by AWS to search for and manage resources across **multiple AWS services** and **multiple AWS Regions** simultaneously using tags. It requires minimal effort from the user (a simple query) and provides a consolidated list quickly, making it the most efficient solution with the least operational overhead.
explanations.correct: The Resource Groups Tag Editor is the fastest and simplest built-in AWS tool to perform global inventory searches based on tags. It abstracts away the complexity of querying individual service APIs in every single Region.

references: AWS Resource Groups Tagging API documentation

questions.text: A company needs to export its database once a day to Amazon S3 for other teams to access. The exported object size varies between 2 GB and 5 GB. The S3 access pattern for the data is variable and changes rapidly. The data must be immediately available and must remain accessible for up to 3 months. The company needs the most cost-effective solution that will not increase retrieval time. Which S3 storage class should the company use to meet these requirements?

options.A: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
options.B: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
options.C: S3 Standard
options.D: S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA)

explanations.A: Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering is the most cost-effective solution for data with **variable or rapidly changing access patterns**. It provides automatic tiering (moving between Frequent Access and Infrequent Access tiers) while maintaining the **millisecond latency** and **immediate availability** required by the problem. It is designed precisely to eliminate the need for manual tiering decisions and avoid retrieval charges from using the wrong Infrequent Access tier, thus meeting all requirements cost-effectively.
explanations.B: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval offers millisecond retrieval, but it is optimized for data that is accessed **rarely** (once per quarter) and has a minimum storage duration charge of 90 days. If the access pattern is variable and *frequently changing*, this class would incur higher retrieval costs than Intelligent-Tiering, violating the 'most cost-effective' requirement for variable access.
explanations.C: S3 Standard is designed for **frequently accessed** data. While it meets the immediate availability requirement, it is the most expensive storage class for storing large amounts of data. For data that is only accessed variably over 3 months, it would not be the **most cost-effective** solution.
explanations.D: S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) is designed for data that is accessed **infrequently** (e.g., once a month) but requires millisecond retrieval. If the access pattern is truly *variable* and changes to being frequently accessed, S3 Standard-IA will impose high retrieval fees, making it potentially more expensive than S3 Standard or S3 Intelligent-Tiering, thus failing the 'most cost-effective' requirement for a variable pattern.
explanations.correct: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between two access tiers (Frequent Access and Infrequent Access) without performance impact, eliminating the risk of unexpected retrieval charges associated with manual tiering and making it the ideal choice for data with unpredictable access patterns.

questions.text: A company hosts a marketing website in an on-premises data center. The website consists of static documents and runs on a single server. An administrator updates the website content infrequently and uses an SFTP client to upload new documents. The company decides to host its website on AWS and to use Amazon CloudFront. The company’s solutions architect creates a CloudFront distribution. The solutions architect must design the most cost-effective and resilient architecture for website hosting to serve as the CloudFront origin. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create a virtual server by using Amazon Lightsail. Configure the web server in the Lightsail instance. Upload website content by using an SFTP client.
options.B: Create an AWS Auto Scaling group for Amazon EC2 instances. Use an Application Load Balancer. Upload website content by using an SFTP client.
options.C: Create a private Amazon S3 bucket. Use an S3 bucket policy to allow access from a CloudFront origin access identity (OAI). Upload website content by using the AWS CLI.
options.D: Create a public Amazon S3 bucket. Configure AWS Transfer for SFTP. Configure the S3 bucket for website hosting. Upload website content by using the SFTP client.

explanations.A: Amazon Lightsail is a simple, fixed-cost VPS (Virtual Private Server). While cost-effective, it requires managing an underlying OS and web server, which increases **operational overhead** and offers less inherent resilience and scalability than a serverless solution like S3.
explanations.B: Using EC2 instances with an Auto Scaling group and an ALB is an architecture for a **dynamic** website. It introduces significant operational overhead and cost (EC2, ALB, EBS, ASG) and is overkill for simple static documents. This is not the *most* cost-effective or simplest solution.
explanations.C: Hosting static content in a private Amazon S3 bucket, secured by a CloudFront Origin Access Identity (OAI), is the industry standard for the **most cost-effective and resilient** static website architecture on AWS. S3 is serverless, highly durable (resilient), and cost-effective. While the original method of uploading was SFTP, the requirement is to meet the architecture goals, and using the AWS CLI (or console, SDK) is the standard and simple method for managing S3 content, minimizing cost and overhead. The use of an OAI ensures content can only be accessed via CloudFront (security).
explanations.D: This solution addresses the customer's preferred upload method (SFTP) by adding AWS Transfer Family for SFTP (an additional cost). However, configuring a **public** S3 bucket for website hosting is less secure than using a private bucket with an OAI (Option C), and AWS Transfer Family adds significant cost and complexity, making it less **cost-effective** overall.
explanations.correct: Amazon S3 provides highly durable, available, and scalable object storage at a very low cost, making it the ideal choice for static website content (resilience and cost-effectiveness). Combining it with CloudFront using an OAI ensures secure delivery and high performance without the cost and overhead of servers.

questions.text: A company has a highly dynamic batch processing job that uses many Amazon EC2 instances to complete it. The job is stateless in nature, can be started and stopped at any given time with no negative impact, and typically takes upwards of 60 minutes total to complete. The company has asked a solutions architect to design a scalable and cost-effective solution that meets the requirements of the job. What should the solutions architect recommend?

options.A: Implement EC2 Spot Instances.
options.B: Purchase EC2 Reserved Instances.
options.C: Implement EC2 On-Demand Instances.
options.D: Implement the processing on AWS Lambda.

explanations.A: EC2 Spot Instances allow customers to bid on unused EC2 capacity, often at significant discounts (up to 90%) compared to On-Demand prices. The key characteristic of the job—being stateless, interruptible, and tolerant of being stopped and restarted—makes it an ideal use case for Spot Instances, providing maximum cost savings for a highly dynamic, non-critical, scalable batch job.
explanations.B: Reserved Instances (RIs) are suited for workloads with a predictable, steady-state usage (24/7 or a defined schedule) over a 1- or 3-year term. While they save money, they are not suitable for a 'highly dynamic' job that is started/stopped, and they require a long-term commitment.
explanations.C: On-Demand Instances are flexible and can be started/stopped at any time, but they offer no discount. They are the most expensive option and would not meet the company's requirement for a **cost-effective** solution.
explanations.D: AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service where functions have a maximum execution time limit (currently 15 minutes). Since the job typically takes **upwards of 60 minutes**, Lambda is not a viable option due to the time constraint.
explanations.correct: EC2 Spot Instances provide the deepest discount and are perfect for highly dynamic, fault-tolerant, and stateless workloads like this batch processing job, as they can handle interruptions and restarts without negative impact.

questions.text:
A company designed a stateless two-tier application that uses Amazon EC2 in a single Availability Zone and an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance. New company management wants to ensure the application is highly available.

What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement?

options.A: Configure the application to use Multi-AZ EC2 Auto Scaling and create an Application Load Balancer
options.B: Configure the application to take snapshots of the EC2 instances and send them to a different AWS Region
options.C: Configure the application to use Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing to feed requests to the application
options.D: Configure Amazon Route 53 rules to handle incoming requests and create a Multi-AZ Application Load Balancer

explanations.A: Correct. Multi-AZ Auto Scaling with an Application Load Balancer ensures EC2-level high availability for a stateless application.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Snapshots are for backup and disaster recovery, not real-time high availability.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Latency-based routing does not address single-AZ failures.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Route 53 rules alone do not replace the need for Auto Scaling across multiple AZs.
explanations.correct: High availability for stateless applications requires Multi-AZ compute with load balancing.

questions.text:
A company uses a three-tier web application to provide training to new employees. The application is accessed for only 12 hours every day. The company is using an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance to store information and wants to minimize costs.
What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.A: Configure an IAM policy for AWS Systems Manager Session Manager. Create an IAM role for the policy. Update the trust relationship of the role. Set up automatic start and stop for the DB instance.
options.B: Create an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cache cluster that gives users the ability to access the data from the cache when the DB instance is stopped. Invalidate the cache after the DB instance is started.
options.C: Launch an Amazon EC2 instance. Create an IAM role that grants access to Amazon RDS. Attach the role to the EC2 instance. Configure a cron job to start and stop the EC2 instance on the desired schedule.
options.D: Create AWS Lambda functions to start and stop the DB instance. Create Amazon EventBridge (Amazon CloudWatch Events) scheduled rules to invoke the Lambda functions. Configure the Lambda functions as event targets for the rules.

explanations.A: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager is used for non-interactive shell access to EC2 instances. It has nothing to do with automating the start and stop of an Amazon RDS DB instance. This option describes an incorrect tool for the required automation task.
explanations.B: While ElastiCache can improve performance, it cannot serve as a reliable substitute for the database when the DB instance is stopped, especially for an application requiring write operations and data persistence. Furthermore, ElastiCache itself is an additional cost component, which contradicts the goal of minimizing costs. The core issue of the DB running 24/7 is not addressed.
explanations.C: Using a separate Amazon EC2 instance with a cron job to run the automation is feasible, but it introduces extra management overhead (managing the EC2 instance, OS, and cron job) and an unnecessary cost (the EC2 instance cost). This is not the most cost-effective or operationally sound solution.
explanations.D: This is the most cost-effective and operationally sound solution. **AWS Lambda** is serverless and can execute the necessary AWS SDK API calls (`start-db-instance` and `stop-db-instance`). **Amazon EventBridge (formerly CloudWatch Events)** provides the built-in, serverless **scheduled rules** capability (cron expression) to precisely trigger the Lambda functions at the required start and stop times (e.g., once at the start of the 12 hours and once at the end). This solution is serverless, highly reliable, and eliminates compute costs for the automation itself, minimizing the overall infrastructure cost.
explanations.correct: The requirement is to save costs on an RDS instance with predictable downtime. Stopping the RDS instance when it's not needed (12 hours per day) is the most effective cost-saving measure. The best practice for scheduling API calls in a serverless, cost-effective manner is to use an **EventBridge (CloudWatch Events) Scheduled Rule** to trigger an **AWS Lambda function** which executes the RDS start/stop API commands.

questions.text: A company wants to run applications in containers in the AWS Cloud. These applications are stateless and can tolerate disruptions within the underlying infrastructure. The company needs a solution that minimizes cost and operational overhead. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.A: Use Spot Instances in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group to run the application containers.
options.B: Use Spot Instances in an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) managed node group.
options.C: Use On-Demand Instances in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group to run the application containers.
options.D: Use On-Demand Instances in an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) managed node group.

explanations.A: This option minimizes cost and operational overhead. **Spot Instances** offer the largest cost savings (up to 90%) for workloads that can tolerate interruptions, which is met by the 'stateless' and 'can tolerate disruptions' requirements. Using an **Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group** is simpler to manage than a full Kubernetes orchestration solution like EKS, thus minimizing operational overhead while still providing scalability. A dedicated container service like ECS/EKS is not strictly necessary for simple scaling and running containers on EC2.
explanations.B: Using Spot Instances in an EKS managed node group is cost-effective, but EKS (Kubernetes) introduces significant operational complexity and overhead compared to a simpler EC2 Auto Scaling group, failing to meet the requirement to **minimize operational overhead**.
explanations.C: Using On-Demand Instances in an Auto Scaling group minimizes operational overhead but is significantly more expensive than using Spot Instances, failing to meet the requirement to **minimize cost**.
explanations.D: Using On-Demand Instances with EKS is the most expensive and complex option. It fails to meet both the requirement to minimize cost (due to On-Demand pricing) and the requirement to minimize operational overhead (due to EKS complexity).
explanations.correct: For stateless, disruption-tolerant applications, Spot Instances offer maximum cost savings. Combining them with a simpler management solution like an EC2 Auto Scaling group (instead of EKS) minimizes operational overhead.

questions.text:
A solutions architect needs to help a company optimize the cost of running an application on AWS. The application will use Amazon EC2 instances, AWS Fargate, and AWS Lambda for compute within the architecture.
The EC2 instances will run the data ingestion layer of the application. EC2 usage will be sporadic and unpredictable. Workloads that run on EC2 instances can be interrupted at any time. The application front end will run on Fargate, and Lambda will serve the API layer. The front-end utilization and API layer utilization will be predictable over the course of the next year.
Which combination of purchasing options will provide the MOST cost-effective solution for hosting this application? (Choose two.)

options.A: Use Spot Instances for the data ingestion layer
options.B: Use On-Demand Instances for the data ingestion layer
options.C: Purchase a 1-year Compute Savings Plan for the front end and API layer.
options.D: Purchase 1-year All Upfront Reserved instances for the data ingestion layer.
options.E: Purchase a 1-year EC2 instance Savings Plan for the front end and API layer.

explanations.A: This is a correct choice. **Spot Instances** provide the largest discount (up to 90% off On-Demand pricing) and are ideal for workloads that are fault-tolerant, stateless, or can be interrupted, which perfectly matches the requirements of the sporadic, unpredictable, and interruptible data ingestion layer.
explanations.B: On-Demand Instances are the most expensive option and should only be used when there is no cost-effective commitment or interruptible option available. This does not meet the requirement for the **MOST cost-effective solution**.
explanations.C: This is a correct choice. A **Compute Savings Plan** offers significant discounts (up to 66% off On-Demand) in exchange for a 1-year or 3-year commitment. Crucially, Compute Savings Plans apply automatically to usage across **EC2, Fargate, and Lambda**, making it the best option for the predictable usage of the Front End (Fargate) and API Layer (Lambda).
explanations.D: Reserved Instances (RIs) are primarily for EC2 instances and do not cover Fargate or Lambda usage, which form part of the predictable workload. Furthermore, RIs are not suitable for the unpredictable and interruptible nature of the data ingestion layer (Spot is better).
explanations.E: An **EC2 Instance Savings Plan** only applies to EC2 usage (and Fargate, but not Lambda) within a specific instance family in a region. The **Compute Savings Plan** (Option C) is more flexible and cost-effective here because it covers Fargate and Lambda without requiring commitment to a specific instance family.
explanations.correct: The best strategy is to use the cheapest option for the interruptible workload (**Spot Instances** for Data Ingestion) and the most flexible commitment option for the predictable, multi-service workload (**Compute Savings Plan** for Fargate/Lambda).

questions.text:
A company recently started using Amazon Aurora as the data store for its global ecommerce application. When large reports are run, developers report that the ecommerce application is performing poorly. After reviewing metrics in Amazon CloudWatch, a solutions architect finds that the ReadIOPS and CPUUtilization metrics are spiking when monthly reports run.
What is the MOST cost-effective solution?

options.A: Migrate the monthly reporting to Amazon Redshift.
options.B: Migrate the monthly reporting to an Aurora Replica.
options.C: Migrate the Aurora database to a larger instance class.
options.D: Increase the Provisioned IOPS on the Aurora instance.

explanations.A: Amazon Redshift is a fully managed, petabyte-scale data warehouse service, ideal for complex analytical processing (OLAP) on massive datasets. While it would solve the performance issue, migrating reporting data to an entirely separate data warehouse system (Redshift) is a significant architectural change that involves ETL/ELT processes and much higher complexity and cost than simply using an existing Aurora feature. It is not the **MOST cost-effective** or operationally simplest solution for offloading read traffic.
explanations.B: **Amazon Aurora Replicas** (Read Replicas) share the same underlying storage volume as the primary instance, allowing them to be deployed quickly and cost-effectively. They are designed to offload read-heavy workloads, like large reports, from the primary database instance. This isolates the reporting spike in ReadIOPS and CPUUtilization from the live ecommerce application, resolving the performance issue with minimal additional cost and operational overhead.
explanations.C: Migrating to a larger instance class (scaling up) would solve the performance issue by increasing the capacity of the *entire* database cluster. However, this increases the cost of the primary instance (which runs 24/7) unnecessarily, even when reports are not running. Using an Aurora Replica (option B) is more cost-effective because you only scale the *read capacity* that is needed for the reports, and you can potentially scale the replica down or terminate it when not in use.
explanations.D: Amazon Aurora is a highly scalable, distributed storage system, and its I/O performance is generally based on the instance class and the cluster volume size, not by manually provisioning IOPS like with traditional RDS on GP3 or io1. You cannot simply 'increase the Provisioned IOPS' for an Aurora cluster. Furthermore, the goal is to isolate the workload, not just increase the capacity of the primary instance.
explanations.correct: The problem is caused by a resource contention between the high-volume ecommerce application and the high-resource reporting workload. The standard, most cost-effective solution for read-heavy operations like reporting on an Amazon Aurora cluster is to use an **Aurora Replica (Read Replica)**. The replica handles all read traffic, isolating the high ReadIOPS and CPUUtilization from the primary instance that serves the low-latency ecommerce application.

questions.text:
A company hosts a website analytics application on a single Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instance. The analytics software is written in PHP and uses a MySQL database. The analytics software, the web server that provides PHP, and the database server are all hosted on the EC2 instance. The application is showing signs of performance degradation during busy times and is presenting 5xx errors. The company needs to make the application scale seamlessly.
Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Migrate the database to an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. Create an AMI of the web application. Use the AMI to launch a second EC2 On-Demand Instance. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute the load to each EC2 instance.
options.B: Migrate the database to an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. Create an AMI of the web application. Use the AMI to launch a second EC2 On-Demand Instance. Use Amazon Route 53 weighted routing to distribute the load across the two EC2 instances.
options.C: Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB instance. Create an AWS Lambda function to stop the EC2 instance and change the instance type. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm to invoke the Lambda function when CPU utilization surpasses 75%.
options.D: Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB instance. Create an AMI of the web application. Apply the AMI to a launch template. Create an Auto Scaling group with the launch template Configure the launch template to use a Spot Fleet. Attach an Application Load Balancer to the Auto Scaling group.

explanations.A: This option separates the database (**a good practice**) and introduces high availability with an ALB and a second EC2 instance. However, this is a fixed, *manual* scaling solution (only two instances). It does not meet the requirement to **scale seamlessly** based on demand, and using On-Demand instances is not the **MOST cost-effective** way to scale horizontally for web traffic.
explanations.B: This option is similar to A but uses Route 53 weighted routing instead of an ALB. Route 53 provides simple DNS-based load balancing, but it lacks health checks and the ability to scale up/down automatically. It is not an auto-scaling solution and is less robust than an ALB for distributing load for a seamless scaling web application.
explanations.C: This option suggests **vertical scaling** (changing instance type), which creates downtime and is not **seamless**. It also doesn't leverage the full power of Aurora (which is often overkill for a simple migration), and it leaves the application tier as a single point of failure (single EC2 instance). This approach is not scalable or highly available.
explanations.D:
This solution provides the best combination of scalability, high availability, and cost-effectiveness: 
1. **Decoupling the DB:** Migrating the database to **Amazon Aurora** (highly scalable and available managed database). 
2. **Seamless Scaling:** Using an **Auto Scaling Group (ASG)** attached to an **Application Load Balancer (ALB)** allows the compute tier to **scale seamlessly** (scale-out) in response to demand, mitigating the 5xx errors and performance degradation. 
3. **Cost-Effectiveness:** Configuring the launch template to use a **Spot Fleet** (or Spot Instances within the ASG) ensures the compute capacity is acquired at the lowest possible cost, making this the **MOST cost-effective** and functionally complete solution.
explanations.correct: To achieve seamless scaling and high availability, the application tier (EC2) must be decoupled from the data tier (DB) and placed behind a load balancer within an Auto Scaling Group. **Option D** uses an **ALB** for distribution, an **ASG** for seamless horizontal scaling, and **Spot Instances/Fleet** for the **MOST cost-effective** capacity acquisition. The database is moved to a managed, scalable service (Aurora), ensuring the entire solution is performant and highly available.

questions.text:
A company runs a stateless web application in production on a group of Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The application experiences heavy usage during an 8-hour period each business day. Application usage is moderate and steady overnight. Application usage is low during weekends.
The company wants to minimize its EC2 costs without affecting the availability of the application.
Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Use Spot Instances for the entire workload.
options.B: Use Reserved Instances for the baseline level of usage. Use Spot instances for any additional capacity that the application needs.
options.C: Use On-Demand Instances for the baseline level of usage. Use Spot Instances for any additional capacity that the application needs.
options.D: Use Dedicated Instances for the baseline level of usage. Use On-Demand Instances for any additional capacity that the application needs.

explanations.A: Using **Spot Instances** for the entire workload is risky because Spot Instances can be interrupted with only a 2-minute warning when EC2 needs the capacity back. While the application is stateless, the interruptions would still affect availability and user experience, violating the core requirement to minimize costs *without affecting availability*.
explanations.B: This is the most cost-effective and risk-mitigated solution. The application has a predictable, **steady baseline** of moderate overnight/weekend usage (or minimum required capacity). This capacity should be covered by **Reserved Instances (RIs)** or **Savings Plans**, which offer a significant discount (up to 72%) in exchange for a 1- or 3-year commitment, securing the lowest possible price for the required 24/7 capacity. The **peak capacity** during the 8-hour workday period can be covered by **Spot Instances** for the largest discount, as the application is stateless and can tolerate the rare interruption. This combination maximizes cost savings while using RIs to ensure baseline availability.
explanations.C: This uses **On-Demand Instances** for the baseline. While this secures baseline availability, On-Demand instances are the most expensive option. This approach does not fulfill the requirement to **minimize EC2 costs** as effectively as using Reserved Instances/Savings Plans for the stable baseline.
explanations.D: **Dedicated Instances** are the most expensive option, only used when compliance or licensing requirements mandate hardware isolation. Using them for the baseline is financially inefficient. **On-Demand Instances** for the peak is also not the most cost-effective way to handle the temporary increase in load, as Spot Instances are cheaper.
explanations.correct: The architecture should match the instance purchasing option to the workload characteristics. The **baseline** (moderate, predictable, continuous usage) should use **Reserved Instances (RIs) or Savings Plans** for the deepest, guaranteed discount and assured availability. The **peak** (temporary, heavy usage) should use **Spot Instances** for the most cost-effective temporary capacity. This combination minimizes overall cost while ensuring the required availability is always met by the RIs.

questions.text:
A company needs to retain application log files for a critical application for 10 years. The application team regularly accesses logs from the past month for troubleshooting, but logs older than 1 month are rarely accessed. The application generates more than 10 TB of logs per month.
Which storage option meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Store the logs in Amazon S3. Use AWS Backup to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
options.B: Store the logs in Amazon S3. Use S3 Lifecycle policies to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
options.C: Store the logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use AWS Backup to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
options.D: Store the logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use Amazon S3 Lifecycle policies to move logs more than 1 month old to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

explanations.A: Storing in S3 is correct, but **AWS Backup** is primarily designed for centralized backup and recovery of various AWS services (EC2, RDS, etc.). It is not the standard or most cost-effective mechanism to automate the transition of data between S3 storage classes; **S3 Lifecycle policies** are the native, automated, and serverless solution for this task.
explanations.B:
This is the **MOST cost-effective** and best practice solution. 
1. **Amazon S3 (likely S3 Standard or S3 Intelligent-Tiering)** provides the necessary **frequent access** and **low latency** for the logs less than 1 month old.
2. **S3 Lifecycle policies** are the native, automated, and free-to-use feature (other than the transition request cost) used to **automatically move** objects between S3 storage classes based on age.
3. **S3 Glacier Deep Archive** is the **cheapest** storage class, designed specifically for data that is rarely accessed and needs to be retained for 10 years (long-term compliance).
explanations.C: While CloudWatch Logs can be used for logs, its cost for ingestion and long-term retention of massive volumes (10 TB/month) often makes it more expensive than directly storing the logs in S3 for archival purposes. Furthermore, **AWS Backup** is the wrong tool for automating S3 storage class transitions.
explanations.D: This option fails for two reasons: First, using **CloudWatch Logs** for **10 TB of logs per month** is typically more expensive for long-term storage than S3. Second, **S3 Lifecycle policies** only apply to objects *already* in an S3 bucket; they cannot directly manage logs stored in CloudWatch Logs.
explanations.correct: Amazon S3 is the foundation for cost-effective, scalable storage for unstructured data like logs. For a 10-year retention requirement where data access dramatically decreases after 1 month, the strategy is to use S3's low-cost archival tier, **S3 Glacier Deep Archive**. The most efficient and automated way to move the data from the 'hot' S3 Standard tier (for the first month) to the 'cold' S3 Glacier Deep Archive tier is by configuring an **S3 Lifecycle policy** based on the object's age.

questions.text:
A company sells ringtones created from clips of popular songs. The files containing the ringtones are stored in Amazon S3 Standard and are at least 128 KB in size. The company has millions of files, but downloads are infrequent for ringtones older than 90 days. The company needs to save money on storage while keeping the most accessed files readily available for its users.
Which action should the company take to meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Configure S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage for the initial storage tier of the objects.
options.B: Move the files to S3 Intelligent-Tiering and configure it to move objects to a less expensive storage tier after 90 days.
options.C: Configure S3 inventory to manage objects and move them to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-1A) after 90 days.
options.D: Implement an S3 Lifecycle policy that moves the objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-1A) after 90 days.

explanations.A: Configuring S3 Standard-IA as the initial storage tier is incorrect. The files are **frequently downloaded** when they are new (less than 90 days old). S3 Standard-IA has a higher retrieval cost and is designed for data accessed less than once a month, which would lead to higher overall costs for new, popular ringtones.
explanations.B: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves data between two access tiers (Frequent and Infrequent) based on access patterns. While this is an excellent solution when access patterns are *unknown* or *changing*, the access pattern here is **predictable** (frequent for 90 days, then infrequent). Using Intelligent-Tiering introduces a small monitoring and automation charge per object, making it less cost-effective than using a fixed, automated lifecycle policy when the access pattern is clearly defined.
explanations.C: **S3 Inventory** is a reporting tool used to list objects and their metadata for auditing purposes. It can define a list of objects but cannot automatically manage or move objects between storage classes. **S3 Lifecycle policies** are the correct tool for the automated movement.
explanations.D:
This is the **MOST cost-effective** and operationally simplest solution. The access pattern is clearly defined: high frequency for 90 days, then low frequency. 
1. **S3 Standard** is used initially for the **frequently accessed** files, ensuring high availability and low latency with no retrieval charges. 
2. An **S3 Lifecycle policy** automatically transitions the objects to the cost-optimized tier, **S3 Standard-IA**, after 90 days. S3 Standard-IA is designed for data that is infrequently accessed but requires rapid access when needed, and it offers significant storage savings over S3 Standard. Since the files are at least 128 KB, they meet the minimum size requirement for Standard-IA, making this process highly efficient.
explanations.correct: When data access patterns are predictable (e.g., accessed often for the first 90 days, then rarely), the most cost-effective solution is to use an **S3 Lifecycle policy** to automate the transition from the high-cost, high-access tier (**S3 Standard**) to the low-cost, low-access tier (**S3 Standard-IA**). This minimizes storage costs without sacrificing the required ready availability for the most popular files.

questions.text:
An ecommerce company hosts its analytics application in the AWS Cloud. The application generates about 300 MB of data each month. The data is stored in JSON format. The company is evaluating a disaster recovery solution to back up the data. The data must be accessible in milliseconds if it is needed, and the data must be kept for 30 days.
Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.A: Amazon OpenSearch Service (Amazon Elasticsearch Service)
options.B: Amazon S3 Glacier
options.C: Amazon S3 Standard
options.D: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL

explanations.A: Amazon OpenSearch Service is an analytics and search engine, not a cost-effective disaster recovery storage solution for raw JSON files. It is significantly more expensive than S3 and involves managing clusters.
explanations.B: Amazon S3 Glacier is an archive storage class designed for data that is rarely accessed (cold data) and requires retrieval times ranging from minutes to hours. This violates the requirement for **millisecond access**.
explanations.C: Amazon S3 Standard offers high durability, immediate (millisecond) access, and is the most cost-effective solution among the immediate-access services for a small amount of data (300 MB) with a short 30-day retention requirement. The cost difference between S3 Standard and less-frequently accessed tiers (like S3 Intelligent-Tiering or S3 Standard-IA) is negligible for such a small volume, making S3 Standard the simplest and **most cost-effective** service that meets all the access requirements.
explanations.D: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL is a relational database service. It is designed for transactional data and is very expensive compared to S3 for storing raw, static JSON data, especially when used only for a disaster recovery backup.
explanations.correct: Amazon S3 Standard is the only option that is cost-effective for a simple backup, stores raw JSON data, and provides the required **millisecond accessibility**.
